title: Japan confirms Oct. 1 residence-fee jump: permanent residence ¥200,000, renewals up to ¥75,000
summary: Final na ang malaking fee increase sa Japan immigration procedures from October 1, 2026. Counter applications for status change/renewal move from today's flat ¥6,000 to ¥10,000–¥75,000 depending on the period granted, while permanent-residence permission rises from ¥10,000 to ¥200,000. The unusually important transition rule: applications accepted by September 30 keep the old fee even if permission comes after October 1.
why_it_matters: This is not a small inflation adjustment. For foreign residents, the cost of an ordinary renewal can multiply several times, while permanent residence becomes 20x more expensive. The deadline also creates a one-month timing effect: people who are already legitimately eligible and ready to file before September 30 can remain under the old fee schedule, while rushed or premature applications can create their own risk.

claims.text: The revised residence-permission fee schedule takes effect for applications accepted on or after October 1, 2026; applications accepted by September 30 retain the old fee even if approval is issued later.

For counter applications, change-of-status and period-of-stay renewal fees move from a flat ¥6,000 to period-based fees ranging from ¥10,000 to ¥75,000; permanent-residence permission rises from ¥10,000 to ¥200,000.
claims.basis: Cabinet-approved fee schedule reported independently by Jiji and TV Asahi

claims.text: For online change-of-status/renewal applications accepted from October 1, the published fee tiers are ¥10,000, ¥15,000, ¥21,000, ¥27,000, ¥42,000, ¥56,000 and ¥65,000 depending on the period granted, plus a ¥330 or ¥550 payment-processing fee; the pre-October online fee is ¥5,500.

The Immigration Services Agency says the higher ceiling reflects examination costs, broader costs of fair immigration/residence management, comparable overseas fees and flexibility for future inflation; it also says the benefit from immigration-management measures differs with the period of stay, which is why renewal/change fees now vary by granted duration.

Fee reductions or exemptions are available only for specified hardship/special-reason cases; for permanent-residence applicants, the official reduction framework is limited to specified family categories such as spouses or children of Japanese nationals, permanent residents or special permanent residents.

The permanent-residence fee increase is 20x (¥200,000 versus ¥10,000); a 5-year-or-longer counter renewal at ¥75,000 is 12.5x the current ¥6,000 counter fee; a 1-year counter renewal at ¥33,000 is 5.5x.
claims.basis: Simple ratio calculation from the confirmed old and new fee amounts

claims.text: The September 30 grandfathering rule creates a rational incentive to file before the cutoff only for applicants who are already eligible and have a complete application; it does not make a premature or weak application strategically sound.
claims.basis: Inference from the transition rule and normal application-quality risk

claims.text: The policy shifts a materially larger share of immigration-administration cost directly onto foreign residents, especially people seeking long periods of stay or permanent residence; the official Q&A states the policy rationale but does not by itself demonstrate that each fee multiplier is proportional to incremental processing cost for that specific application type.
claims.basis: Distributional and evidence-boundary assessment of the official rationale and fee schedule

reading_levels.30_sec: Japan's Oct. 1 immigration-fee increase is now finalized. Counter renewals/status changes go from ¥6,000 flat to ¥10,000–¥75,000 based on the period granted; permanent residence goes from ¥10,000 to ¥200,000. Crucial cutoff: applications accepted by Sep. 30 keep the old fee even if approved later. If already eligible and documents are genuinely ready, check filing timing now—don't rush a weak application just to save the fee.
reading_levels.2_min: The headline maximum is not every renewal. The new counter fee depends on the period actually granted: examples reported from the final decree include ¥10,000 for three months or less, ¥33,000 for one year, ¥64,000 for three to under five years, and ¥75,000 for five years or more. Online change/renewal remains cheaper than counter filing but also rises sharply: the official table runs from ¥10,000 to ¥65,000 plus a small processing fee, versus ¥5,500 today. Permanent-residence permission is the biggest jump at ¥200,000. The government says foreign residents should bear an appropriate share of strengthened immigration-management costs and cites processing cost, system-wide management expenses, overseas comparisons and inflation. The skeptical point: those factors explain a policy direction, but the public Q&A does not establish a transparent per-case cost model that independently justifies a 20x PR fee.
reading_levels.deep: This is both a cost-policy change and a behavioral deadline. The grandfathering rule is unusually clear: what matters is the application acceptance date, not the permission date. That can accelerate otherwise-ready September filings. But fee avoidance should not override eligibility, document quality or timing rules. Online filing after October 1 also changes payment mechanics: payment is through the designated contractor by convenience-store or bank payment, not credit card/QR, and online applications do not support the fee-reduction procedure. The wider policy signal is also important: Japan is moving away from very low, nearly uniform residence-procedure fees toward duration-linked user charges, explicitly framing immigration management as a service whose growing costs should be borne more directly by foreign residents.

content.whats_new: The May legal change and July proposal are no longer hypothetical: the Cabinet finalized the implementing fee schedule on August 25, and the Immigration Services Agency has now published the October 1 transition, online-payment rules and reduction guidance. The most actionable newly confirmed point is the September 30 grandfathering rule.
content.skeptical_view: Do not compress this into 'every visa renewal becomes ¥75,000.' The amount depends on the period granted and online filing has a lower schedule. Also, the government's justification is broader than pure case-processing cost: it explicitly includes overall immigration/residence-management spending, overseas fee levels and future inflation. That means the increase is partly a policy choice about who should finance the system, not simply a pass-through of a documented per-application cost increase.
content.what_next: Watch whether ISA publishes more detailed operational guidance before October 1, especially on payment handling, reduction cases and any implementation problems. Longer term, watch whether higher fees alter application timing, permanent-residence demand, employer support policies, or renewal behavior—and whether future increases use the new statutory ceiling more aggressively.
content.what_would_change_mind: Upgrade concern if official budget/cost data show the fee increase materially exceeds attributable administrative costs, if employers or resident groups report meaningful access barriers, or if further fee hikes follow quickly. Downgrade concern if detailed cost accounting shows strong proportionality between the new charges and actual system costs, hardship relief proves broad/effective, and application volumes show little access effect. Any official correction to the September 30 transition rule would materially change the immediate recommendation.
content.recommendation: DO NOW only if relevant: check your residence-card expiry and any already-planned status change or permanent-residence filing. If you are already eligible and the application can be complete and properly accepted by September 30, filing before the cutoff can preserve the old fee. Do not submit early solely for fee avoidance if eligibility, tax/pension records, employment documents or other required evidence are not ready. For applications after October 1, compare online versus counter filing because the new online renewal/change schedule is lower, but note the extra payment fee and that reduction requests require counter filing.

pr_vs_reality.official_claim: ISA says stronger and expanded immigration/residence management requires sufficient funding and that foreign residents should bear an appropriate share; the fee design also considers processing cost, overseas fees and inflation.
evidence_says: The increase is large and finalized: permanent residence rises 20x, while ordinary renewal/change fees become duration-based and can rise more than tenfold at the longest counter tier.
The government has created hardship reductions/exemptions, but eligibility is limited and online applications do not support the reduction procedure.
The public Q&A explains the policy criteria but does not, on its face, provide a per-application cost breakdown proving that each multiplier maps directly to incremental processing cost.
pr_vs_reality.verdict: Real administrative-funding rationale, but also a major distributional policy shift: foreign residents will directly finance much more of the system, and the September 30 cutoff makes the change immediately actionable.
